# There's More to Your Child Than School Can Measure

*The founder's six-part series, for publication on truermeasure.com as a single page (proposed route: /more). Source for the Monday series in the content calendar. Verbatim; do not edit.*

---

## Part 1 — What Hasn't Changed

It's back-to-school season.

And once again, we're having big conversations about phones and AI in schools.

What kids should have access to. What they shouldn't. What we should restrict. What we should embrace. And what they need to learn to use well.

Those conversations matter.

But I wonder if, in all our attention to what is changing, we're forgetting to pay attention to **what hasn't changed at all.**

Kids still want to be seen.

They want someone to notice what they're good at.

They want to feel understood.

They want to belong.

They want adults who are genuinely interested in them.

They want to laugh.

They want to make things.

They want to talk to each other.

They want to be challenged without constantly feeling judged.

They want to become good at things that matter to them.

They want to be inspired by people who make them curious about something they didn't know they cared about.

Technology can change enormously.

**Human beings don't change nearly that fast.**

And I think that matters as we send kids back to school.

Because while we debate phones, AI, and whatever technology comes next, we should also be asking:

**What do kids need that no technology can replace?**

I don't think the answer is to pretend these technologies don't exist. Kids are growing up in a world with them. Part of education should be helping them learn to use them well.

But education has to come first.

The relationships. The curiosity. The thinking. The conversation. The sense of belonging. The desire to learn.

**Those are the things technology should serve, not replace.**

## Part 2 — There's more to your child than school can measure

Soon, there will be numbers.

Grades. Test scores. Attendance. Rubrics. Assessments.

And those things can tell you something about your child.

But they cannot tell you everything.

After 25 years in education, first as a teacher and then as a principal, this is one of the things I wish more parents understood:

**There's more to your child than school can measure.**

Not because schools don't care about the rest.

Because some of the most important things about a child are incredibly difficult to capture on a report card.

Curiosity.

Original thinking.

The courage to question something that doesn't make sense.

The ability to make people laugh.

Knowing when someone else needs a friend.

Getting completely absorbed in something they care about.

Making things.

Fixing things.

Leading without being asked.

Trying again after something goes badly.

Seeing possibilities other people don't see yet.

None of those things fit particularly neatly into a percentage.

And that matters.

## Part 3 — We've become very good at measuring what school needs to know

Schools need information.

Teachers need to know whether children can read, write, understand mathematical concepts, communicate their thinking, and meet curriculum expectations.

Assessment has a purpose.

I'm not arguing that we should stop measuring academic learning.

I'm asking us to notice something else:

**What happens when the things we can measure become the things we pay the most attention to?**

Because eventually, a subtle shift can happen.

A child gets a 72 in math, and suddenly the 72 starts carrying more weight than the way she spent Saturday afternoon figuring out how something worked.

A child struggles to sit still during a lesson, while nobody records the fact that he can spend three uninterrupted hours building something he chose himself.

Another gets excellent grades and looks successful on paper, while quietly becoming less curious about anything that won't be on the test.

The measurements aren't necessarily wrong.

**They're incomplete.**

And incomplete information becomes a problem when we forget that it's incomplete.

## Part 4 — A report card measures performance in a particular environment

A report card can tell you something about how your child is performing within school.

It cannot fully tell you who your child is.

Those are not the same question.

I've known children who were extraordinary thinkers but mediocre test takers.

Children who could command a room but struggled to complete worksheets.

Children whose creativity appeared everywhere except in the places we happened to assess it.

And I've known children who were exceptionally good at school.

They understood expectations. They completed the work. They earned excellent grades.

But doing well in school and loving learning are not always the same thing.

Sometimes "I want to know" slowly becomes:

"Is this on the test?"

Or:

"Does this count?"

That should make us curious.

Because education should not only be preparing children to succeed at school.

Eventually, school ends.

## Part 5 — Parents need to notice what school can't

This is where I think parents have an incredibly important role.

Not to become another teacher at home.

Not to monitor every grade.

Not to turn childhood into one giant exercise in maximizing potential.

But to notice.

What makes your child lose track of time?

What do they teach themselves without being asked?

What problems do they notice?

What questions do they keep asking?

What comes easily to them that they assume comes easily to everyone?

When do other kids naturally follow them?

What do they make, organize, invent, repair, perform, explain, collect, research, negotiate, or obsess over?

When do you see a version of your child that might never appear on a report card?

Because children are constantly giving us information about who they are becoming.

We just need to make sure the things that are easiest to measure don't become the only things we learn to see.

## Part 6 — This back-to-school season, keep looking

When the report card eventually comes home, read it.

Take it seriously.

Celebrate progress.

Ask questions when something concerns you.

Help where help is needed.

But don't accidentally hand that document more authority than it deserves.

If the grades are excellent, keep looking.

If the grades are struggling, keep looking.

If your child fits beautifully into school, keep looking.

If your child doesn't, **keep looking.**

Because maybe one of the most important questions we can ask about a child isn't:

**"How are they doing in school?"**

It's:

**"What are we learning about who they are becoming?"**

Phones will change.

AI will change.

The jobs we're preparing children for will change.

School itself will change.

But a child wanting to be seen, understood, challenged, connected, and inspired?

**I don't think we should lose sight of that while we're busy debating everything else.**

There's more to your child than school can measure.

This year, make sure you notice it.
